intro_script: Welcome to your daily research digest for November 26, 2026. Today we cover breakthroughs in autonomous systems, adversarial attacks, and prompt injection techniques. Tune in for the latest.
outro_script: And that's all the research news for today, November 26th, 2026! May your algorithms be wisely governed. Until tomorrow, keep those insights sharp, and I'll catch you in the next digest.

items.title: Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition
items.summary: Allocation of resources is a structural component of agent governance, introducing trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and strategy-proofness. Impossibility results demonstrate that these allocation constraints cannot be resolved in a single control layer. This necessitates a multi-scale governance structure involving temporal atomicity, state enforcement, behavioral monitoring, and population allocation. An irreducibility theorem states that no architecture can eliminate these dimensions without sacrificing correctness or stability. Ultimately, agent governance is reframed as a structural problem concerning how access to execution is determined.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition" outlines the necessity of a complex governance structure for autonomous agent systems, demonstrating that resource allocation involves inherent trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and strategy-proofness. The research establishes that resolving these allocation constraints cannot occur within a single control layer, necessitating a multi-scale governance structure incorporating temporal atomicity, state enforcement, behavioral monitoring, and population allocation. An irreducibility theorem is presented, stating that no architecture can eliminate these dimensions without sacrificing correctness or stability, reframing agent governance as a structural problem concerning the determination of execution access. This work suggests a need for layered architectural solutions in designing robust autonomous agent systems.

items.title: Antares-Smaug: Adversarial Names, Tokens and Attack Rewrites: Sanitisers Miss Unseen Generalisations
items.summary: Researchers attacked six Laya models using 81 programmatic edits and 566 synthetic items to test their robustness. Attacks leveraging adversarial names significantly influenced the released model's answers, with option naming steering results in 32% of cases. Sanitizers failed to capture these unseen generalizations, as freezing them reduced attack effectiveness by 72% but not fully preventing attacks. An attacker selecting the best strings restored success to 84%, demonstrating vulnerabilities in current defenses. The study indicates that existing sanitizers miss important attack vectors related to naming and character edits.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Antares-Smaug: Adversarial Names, Tokens and Attack Rewrites: Sanitisers Miss Unseen Generalisations" reports on research into the robustness of language models against adversarial attacks. Researchers tested six Laya models using eighty-one programmatic edits and five hundred sixty-six synthetic items to assess their resilience. Attacks utilizing adversarial names demonstrated a significant influence on the released model's outputs, with option naming steering results in thirty-two percent of cases. The study found that existing sanitizers failed to capture these unseen generalizations, although freezing these mechanisms reduced attack effectiveness by seventy-two percent. An attacker selecting the optimal strings restored success rates to eighty-four percent, indicating vulnerabilities in current defense mechanisms. This research highlights the necessity for updating sanitization techniques to address subtle variations in naming and character edits. The findings suggest a need for more comprehensive defense strategies against sophisticated model manipulation.

items.title: ContextLure: Exploiting Benign Conversation History for Indirect Prompt Injection
items.summary: Attackers can exploit benign conversation history to perform indirect prompt injection attacks against LLMs. The ContextLure framework allows an attacker to silently observe and extract evidence from existing conversations. To effectively exploit this, the framework selects evidence based on user/system preferences and uses an urgency/priority matrix for crafting malicious requests. Experimental results showed attackers could leverage benign interaction evidence for later attacks with notable success rates. This demonstrates a vulnerability in agent interactions where prior context can be misused for malicious purposes.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "ContextLure: Exploiting Benign Conversation History for Indirect Prompt Injection" details a method for exploiting existing conversation history to perform indirect prompt injection attacks against large language models. The ContextLure framework enables an attacker to silently observe and extract evidence from prior interactions by selecting evidence based on user or system preferences and employing an urgency and priority matrix when formulating malicious requests. Experimental results indicated that attackers successfully leveraged benign interaction evidence to execute subsequent attacks with notable success rates. This demonstrates a vulnerability in agent interactions where prior context can be misused for malicious purposes. The research suggests a need for enhanced security measures concerning the management and isolation of conversational context within AI systems.

items.title: What People Choose Not to Say: A Multimodal Benchmark for Fine-Grained Information Manipulation in Conversations
items.summary: Existing benchmarks for social understanding often focus on coarse-grained emotion or binary truth-deception, neglecting finer manipulation tactics in conversations. This paper introduces InfoCon, a multimodal benchmark designed to assess fine-grained information manipulation strategies such as withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim. The benchmark uses an evidence-grounded multi-agent annotation framework to reliably label these complex conversational behaviors. It allows for a systematic analysis of how multimodal models understand these nuanced manipulation tactics. Ultimately, the work provides a testing ground beyond simple truth-deception judgments for evaluating AI's conversational understanding.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "What People Choose Not to Say: A Multimodal Benchmark for Fine-Grained Information Manipulation in Conversations" introduces a multimodal benchmark designed to assess fine-grained information manipulation strategies within conversations. The research establishes a framework to systematically evaluate how multimodal models understand nuanced conversational manipulation tactics beyond simple truth-deception judgments. The methodology involves an evidence-grounded multi-agent annotation framework to reliably label complex conversational behaviors such as withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim. This approach moves beyond coarse-grained assessments to provide a testing ground for evaluating AI conversational understanding. The work provides a necessary tool for analyzing the depth of multimodal model comprehension in complex dialogue scenarios. This research signals a shift in evaluating artificial intelligence capabilities toward recognizing subtle conversational deceit.

items.title: Taxi: Analyzing Agents at (Real) Scale
items.summary: Taxi is a system designed for debugging, clustering, and monitoring agents at scale, efficiently handling millions of steps. It primarily uses clustering to create a taxonomy of steps and provides full SQL access for complex querying by engineers and agents. The system employs a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent and experiments with Jev-style decision models for semantic routing. Taxi is designed to be modular and extensible, featuring built-in evaluators and daily reports.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Taxi: Analyzing Agents at (Real) Scale" details a system designed for debugging, clustering, and monitoring agents at scale, achieving efficiency across millions of steps through clustering. The system utilizes a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent and experiments with Jev-style decision models for semantic routing. It employs clustering to create a taxonomy of steps and grants full SQL access for complex querying by engineers and agents. Furthermore, the system is modular and extensible, incorporating built-in evaluators and daily reports. This research presents a framework for managing the complexity inherent in large-scale agent workflows. Future developments in agent supervision and scale management are expected to build upon these analytical methods.

items.title: Beyond Static Charts: Benchmarking Interactive Chart-to-Code Generation for MLLMs
items.summary: Existing benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in chart-to-code generation primarily focus on static charts, ignoring interactive chart exploration. ChartInt, a new benchmark, was introduced to specifically evaluate interactive generation by including examples of common interaction patterns and editing tasks. A preset state snapshot protocol was developed to ensure reproducible evaluation of dynamic interaction behaviors. The evaluation framework measures both semantic and stylistic consistency in these interactive scenarios. Experiments demonstrate that MLLMs perform significantly worse on interactive tasks compared to static chart generation.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Beyond Static Charts: Benchmarking Interactive Chart-to-Code Generation for MLLMs" details a new benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of multimodal large language models to generate code from interactive charts. The research introduced ChartInt, a benchmark that specifically assesses interactive generation by incorporating examples of common interaction patterns and editing tasks, utilizing a preset state snapshot protocol to ensure reproducible evaluation of dynamic interaction behaviors. The evaluation framework measures both semantic and stylistic consistency across these interactive scenarios. Experiments revealed that multimodal large language models exhibit significantly poorer performance on interactive tasks when compared to generating code from static charts. This finding indicates a gap in current evaluation methods for assessing the dynamic reasoning capabilities of MLLMs in multimodal tasks.

items.title: REI: Learning Ideation from Repository Evolution
items.summary: Ideation in science and engineering is bottlenecked by the cost of exploration, which is addressed by learning from repository evolution. The proposed REI framework learns reusable ideation policies by analyzing code changes and subsequent reuse in repositories. A limitation identified is semantic diversity collapse, where generated ideas cluster in dominant method families, hindering generalization. Semantic Prior Optimization and Debiasing (SPOD) is introduced to mitigate this by making method identity explicit and correcting reward bias. Experiments show that REI with SPOD improves ideation quality, method diversity, and cross-task generalization.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "REI: Learning Ideation from Repository Evolution" reports on a framework designed to learn reusable ideation policies by analyzing code changes and subsequent reuse across repositories. The research introduces the REI framework to address the cost of exploration in science and engineering by learning from repository evolution. The methodology involves analyzing code changes to learn policies for idea generation, which naturally led to an identified limitation known as semantic diversity collapse where generated ideas cluster in dominant method families. To counter this, Semantic Prior Optimization and Debiasing, or SPOD, are introduced to make method identity explicit and correct reward bias during the learning process. Experiments demonstrate that the REI system incorporating SPOD improves ideation quality, method diversity, and cross-task generalization. This work suggests a method for generating more diverse and generalized scientific and engineering ideas through automated repository analysis.

items.title: SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents
items.summary: Spatial reasoning agents often struggle with orchestrating external tools like 3D reconstruction and segmentation. SpatialCraft is a self-evolving framework designed to improve the orchestration of these tools using experience and skills. It maintains "Experiences," distilled from contrasting rollouts, and "Skills," defined by explicit conditions. A Contrastive Utility Score is used to estimate the effect of experiences, consolidating positive ones into skills. The framework demonstrates that a frozen agent can learn effective spatial tool orchestration from its own interaction history.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents" details a self-evolving framework designed to improve the orchestration of external spatial tools through experience and skills. The research demonstrates that a frozen agent can learn effective spatial tool orchestration directly from its interaction history. The SpatialCraft framework maintains experiences distilled from contrasting rollouts and skills defined by explicit conditions. A Contrastive Utility Score is employed to assess the impact of these experiences, consolidating positive instances into formalized skills. The methodology shows that this process allows agents to learn complex sequences of actions necessary for tasks like 3D reconstruction and segmentation by leveraging their own interaction history. This development indicates a pathway toward more robust and adaptive spatial reasoning capabilities in artificial intelligence systems.

items.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
items.summary: MOZAIC is a paired benchmark designed to measure the contribution of audio and video modalities to deepfake detection. It provides 137,745 clips with a four-way label indicating real/fake combinations for both video and audio. The benchmark covers deepfakes involving face swapping, video diffusion, and voice conversion. Evaluation showed that multimodal LLMs performed well, and detectors achieved high accuracy, though generalization remains an open question. The authors release the dataset, a smaller split, code, and prompts for further research.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake" details a paired benchmark designed to measure the contribution of audio and video modalities to deepfake detection, showing that multimodal large language models performed well in evaluation. The research presents a dataset comprising 137,745 clips featuring deepfakes involving face swapping, video diffusion, and voice conversion, each labeled with a four-way designation of real or fake for both the audio and video components. Evaluation of this benchmark indicated that detectors achieved high accuracy, although the capacity for generalization across different deepfake types remains an area requiring further investigation. The authors have released the benchmark dataset, a smaller subset, the accompanying code, and research prompts for broader study. This work provides a structured means for assessing multimodal deepfake detection capabilities in the current artificial intelligence landscape.

items.title: KiRA: Kronecker Input-Gated Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pretrained Models
items.summary: KiRA introduces Kronecker input-gated rank adaptation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of pretrained models. It modifies low-rank updates by using the Kronecker product of a frozen matrix and a trainable input-dependent factor. An input gate $g(x)$ adjusts the rank of the update in discrete steps, allowing for input conditioning without increasing trainable parameters. This method demonstrated superior performance on six benchmarks compared to low-rank adaptation, requiring 8.7--9.7 times fewer trainable parameters. The approach successfully predicted the benefit of input conditioning based on labeled data.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "KiRA: Kronecker Input-Gated Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pretrained Models" details a method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of pretrained models. The research introduces Kronecker input-gated rank adaptation to modify low-rank updates using the Kronecker product of a frozen matrix and a trainable input-dependent factor. This method incorporates an input gate, g(x), which adjusts the rank of the update in discrete steps, enabling input conditioning without increasing trainable parameters. Evaluations on six benchmarks showed that this approach achieved superior performance compared to standard low-rank adaptation, requiring eight point seven to nine point seven times fewer trainable parameters. This technique demonstrated the predicted benefit of input conditioning based on labeled data. The development indicates a pathway for more efficient and context-aware fine-tuning of large pretrained models.

items.title: The Symmetry Budget: How Much Group Structure Should a Network Architecture Assume?
items.summary: Network architectures often rely on symmetry assumptions, such as convolution tying weights across translations. The paper investigates how much group structure a network should assume based on data symmetry. It analyzes a solvable model using linear maps over the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_d$ to study the trade-off between approximation and estimation error. The study shows that intermediate architectures are generally not optimal, pointing towards a phase boundary for optimality. Structured defects in symmetry can restore optimal performance, and the findings are validated by experimental measurements.

items.title: Centered Kernel Distance: Dimension-Free Error Bounds for Comparing Neural Representations
items.summary: The Centered Kernel Distance (CKD) is introduced as a natural metric counterpart to representational similarity measures like CKA and RSA. The study demonstrates that CKD admits an unbiased estimator, unlike several popular similarity measures such as CKA. Estimation error for CKD decays proportionally to $1/M + 1/N$, independent of the dimensionality of experimental conditions. This finding shows that similarity estimation avoids the curse of dimensionality. Empirical verification was conducted across various neural network and biological data.

items.title: Understanding Double Descent through Universal Compression
items.summary: Deep learning models often exhibit a double-descent phenomenon, where test loss peaks near the interpolation threshold before decreasing again, defying classical bias-variance predictions. This paper interprets this phenomenon using the concept of universal compression. The authors bound the maximum-likelihood excess test loss by summing four terms, including an approximation-and-shift term and a minimax batch regret. Experiments suggest that the gap between Maximum Likelihood Estimation and the Bayes predictor significantly contributes to the double-descent peak. Specifically, using a Gaussian-prior SGLD approximation shows no pronounced interpolation peak, but the gap is a major factor under uniform random labels.

items.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
items.summary: The work seeks quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity for language generation, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory. It studies a PAC model where a learner must output a sampler whose distribution is close to the uniform distribution over the target language. The research investigates whether specific ingredients, like online learnability, are necessary for this learning. The authors construct a concept class where online learning is hard but PAC learning to sample is efficient. New algorithms are developed utilizing offline oracles and approximate sampling oracles for concept intersections.

items.title: Adversarial Bandit Convex Optimization with $d^{3/2}\sqrt{n}$ Regret
items.summary: The paper studies adversarial bandit convex optimization where a learner selects points in a convex body and observes noisy convex loss values. The losses are manipulated by an adversary who adapts to the learner's past actions. The authors improve the regret bound for this problem to $\widetilde O(d^{3/2}\sqrt n)$, matching conjectured rates. This result, combined with a lower bound, determines the minimax regret up to a factor of $d^{1/6}$. The method employs an online Newton step with Gaussian exploration, using unbiased gradient and Hessian estimates.

items.title: Attributing Agentic Failure in Reasoning Vision-Language Models with Interactive 2D Environments
items.summary: Agentic benchmarks show varied failure causes, such as misreading the environment or failing to recover from mistakes. The research introduces MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld, an interactive 2D maze designed for failure attribution. This environment incorporates mechanisms like key-door pairs and switch-gate pairs to test reasoning. A breadth-first search method is used to determine the optimal action count, which helps grade unfinished episodes. The study evaluates three vision-language models on these environments to analyze agentic failure.

items.title: Code availability is not enough: schemas for documenting and extending data analysis
items.summary: Reproducing data analysis requires understanding the sequence of decisions, not just the code. The proposed work introduces a schema to represent a data analysis as a collection of natural language decisions. This schema allows large language models to generate and validate analysis scripts directly from the documentation. It enables expanding a single analysis into a multiverse of alternatives for comparison. Demonstrations show this workflow can reproduce results and automatically generate alternative code.

items.title: Semantic Density Does Not Predict Agent-Memory Collapse
items.summary: Persistent textual memory can help LLM agents, but repeated updates can degrade task performance. Research investigated whether memory statistics predict early declines in task accuracy. Various measures, including cosine similarity, geometry, and graph statistics, did not reliably predict task performance decline. Classifiers trained on these statistics failed to accurately flag memory collapse in real-world agent runs. The study concludes that global semantic density and local crowding did not serve as reliable warnings for agent-memory collapse.

items.title: Neighbor Crowding Predicts Feature Stability in Sparse Autoencoders
items.summary: Sparse Autoencoders aim to identify stable language model representations by breaking down features. The study investigates feature stability across different training token levels using computationally cheap statistics instead of training multiple seeds. Neighbor crowding, a geometric property of the dictionary, is identified as the strongest predictor of feature stability. Features located in dense regions of the unit sphere are more likely to be stable than isolated ones. This work provides a method to predict feature stability without the expense of training multiple SAE seeds.

items.title: Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data
items.summary: The Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model is proposed to address attribute reduction in incomplete information systems where missing values complicate rough set theory. COFRS defines object similarity based on a weighted overlap of present attributes, penalizing missing values globally. This similarity is used to define a soft dependency degree via weighted granule consistency, and reducts are found using greedy backward elimination. Benchmarks show COFRS selects smaller reducts on average compared to other methods, emphasizing compactness over predictive accuracy.

items.title: Improved Sample Complexity of Robust Reinforcement Learning with KL Uncertainty Sets
items.summary: The paper studies distributionally robust reinforcement learning using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The objective is to find a policy that maximizes the worst-case value over all possible transition kernels within the uncertainty set. The authors develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for the sample complexity of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal robust policy. The new upper bound improves upon existing results by an order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-1}\})$. Furthermore, the lower bound holds across all uncertainty levels, showing better agreement between the bounds.

items.title: Geophysics-informed invertible operator network for Bayesian geophysical inversion
items.summary: Geophysical inverse problems are ill-posed, making classical Bayesian methods computationally expensive. A geophysics-informed invertible operator network (GI-ION) is proposed to efficiently perform Bayesian geophysical inversion. This method integrates an invertible neural network to learn the forward operator and represent uncertainty via latent variables. GI-ION enables efficient sampling from a learned conditional approximation even with sparse observations. Validation on 1D surface-wave dispersion and travel-time tomography demonstrated robust performance.

items.title: Deep Learning-Based Mesoscopic Emission Modeling
items.summary: Existing emission models face a trade-off between efficiency and accuracy, necessitating a better approach for urban air pollution. Direct Emission Prediction (DEP), a GRU-based deep learning model, is introduced to predict $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{NO}_x$ emissions from link-level inputs. Trained on synthetic data, DEP matches the accuracy of a hybrid reference model within acceptable error margins while significantly reducing computational time. Validation shows DEP accurately reproduces real-world $\text{NO}_x$ levels and effectively captures spatial cold-start emission hotspots. This work demonstrates that deep learning can achieve microscopic accuracy at lower computational cost for scalable urban emission modeling.

items.title: Temporal Exposure to Byzantine Vulnerability Under Intermittent Participation in Federated Learning
items.summary: Dynamic Participation Exposure (DPE) is introduced to study Byzantine vulnerability when client participation varies in Federated Learning. Intermittent participation transforms Byzantine robustness from a static property into a stochastic and temporal one. The study analyzes the probability of per-round exposure based on the active-set size and examines the accumulation of exposure over multiple rounds. Intermittent participation alone does not guarantee aggregation failure, but it necessitates new mitigation strategies. Actionable recommendations include constraints on active sets, temporal monitoring, and adaptive aggregation techniques.

items.title: On the Impact of Extra Information in Bandit Learning: More is Not Always Merrier
items.summary: More data is not always beneficial for learning performance in sequential decision-making settings. The paper investigates whether extra reward samples in stochastic bandit setups guarantee a reduction in regret. The widely used Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm is shown to violate this property, experiencing higher regret with extra information under certain benign conditions. Thompson Sampling and Explore-Then-Commit appear to benefit from this extra information. A meta-algorithm is proposed to ensure non-degradation for a broad class of bandit algorithms.

items.title: Learning What vs. Learning How: Decomposing Task and Interface Competence in Agentic Training
items.summary: Agentic competence is decomposed into task competence, the knowledge to solve a task, and interface competence, the ability to act on that knowledge via a specific harness. The study investigates how training methods, conditioned by these harness structures, affect the development of these two competencies. Multi-harness distillation aggregates task knowledge but requires preserving interface competence for the knowledge to be realized. Harness rehearsal, combining task supervision and interface exercise, yields significantly better results than either alone. Policy reinforcement learning proves more robust than distillation for single-harness training in maintaining interface competence.

items.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Signature Forgery Detection
items.summary: This work explores quantum machine learning pipelines for offline signature forgery detection using public image data. It employs a ZZ feature map quantum kernel paired with classical learners like K-Nearest Neighbors and Support Vector Machine. A hybrid approach utilizes a frozen EfficientNetB0 for feature extraction followed by a quantum-compatible principal component projection. This hybrid method achieved 92.62% accuracy on a held-out test fold and 91.26% mean accuracy across five-fold cross-validation. The proposed pipeline maintains a quantum embedding step suitable for NISQ hardware.

items.title: A Causal Energy Prior for Learning Directed Acyclic Graphs
items.summary: Bayesian learning of Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) often uses non-informative priors, which lack directional causal information. The proposed local-global energy prior (LGE) is a Gibbs distribution that combines local divergence, Structural Hamming Distance, and a causal Structural Intervention Distance. Rules are derived to calibrate the decay and weighting of these divergences based on the prior DAG. Simulations show that LGE improves the structural accuracy of maximum a posteriori DAGs and the fit of the resulting Bayesian networks. This method was demonstrated on a gene regulatory network learned from single-cell kidney data.

items.title: Evaluating Ensemble Methods for Algorithmic Stability Under Data Perturbations
items.summary: Ensembling methods can destabilize classifiers that are already stable, although subbagging improves stability in certain settings. The effect of ensembling on stability depends on the perturbation level, introducing Monte Carlo noise that slowly decreases with more bags. The Rashomon set, representing models with near-optimal performance, can stabilize unstable classifiers by using predictive multiplicity. However, this stabilization is not guaranteed and is not a general replacement for subbagging. Results suggest ensemble methods stabilize unstable classifiers via influence equalization, but the mechanism differs for stable classifiers.

items.title: Gaussian priors from nonlinear PDEs with the semiclassical approximation
items.summary: Probabilistic methods for solving partial differential equations treat the problem as a Bayesian inverse problem, often employing Gaussian priors for field reconstruction. This work utilizes the semiclassical approximation to construct Gaussian priors from variational energies or integrated square residuals for nonlinear PDEs. The prior is derived by expanding the PDE energy around a stable solution to uncover a Gaussian form. The covariance operator of the prior is determined by the inverse of the Hessian of the energy associated with the PDE solution space. The resulting prior's response to model-form error depends on the distance between the assumed model and the ground truth.
